No prompt-injection attempts were seen. No Bash, downloads or code copying.

Key findings:
1. Entrance holes are smaller than the bullet: 9 mm at 1.6 m made 5.61±0.57 mm holes in belly skin and 3.33±1.17 mm in back skin, about 0.37–0.62 × calibre (Geisenberger 2022, PMID 36006518).
2. 72% of 5.56 entrances were smaller than the bullet, with micro-tears and no abrasion collar (Bangkok 2010, PMID 27890096).
3. Abrasion-ring area to hole area is 3:1 for .22 LR and 2.45:1 for 9 mm (PMID 1811497). That gives a collar about 2–2.5 mm wide for 9 mm (derived). The collar is eccentric, widest on the side facing the shooter, in angled shots (StatPearls NBK556119).
4. Collar width peaks at intermediate velocity and scales with bullet diameter (Randall & Jaqua 1991, PMID 2007864). Round-nose bullets make the largest rings and smallest holes; wadcutters the opposite (Pircher 2017, PMID 27909866).
5. Soot reaches about 20–30 cm with handguns and is gone by about 40 cm; rifles roughly double this (PathologyOutlines / Medscape / forensicmed). Stippling with a .38 reaches 45–60 cm (flake powder), 90 cm (flattened ball) and 120 cm (ball) (DiMaio 1976). The stipple pattern is 5.7–17.6 cm wide at 30 cm and at least 16.5 cm at 61 cm (ETSU thesis). Stipples are red-orange in the living and grey-yellow if the body was already dead.
6. Contact over bone: gas under the scalp causes a stellate tear, a muzzle imprint (seen forming on high-speed video) and cherry-red CO tissue. .22 LR rarely makes true stellate tears; .357 Magnum makes large ones (ACEP Now; skin-skull-brain model).
7. Exit shapes: circular 31.6%, stellate 27.6%, irregular 24.5%, slit 12.2%, crescent 4.1%; head exits skew stellate or irregular (Pipatchotitham). Rifle exit size depends on the temporary cavity at the exit plane (PMID 23700297).
8. Skull: inward bevel at the entrance, outward at the exit; bone exits were larger in 16 of 17 cases; thin bones show no bevel (Quatrehomme & Işcan 1998, PMID 9670492). Skull thickness: frontal about 8 mm, parietal 7–10 mm, temporal about 4.7 mm (as thin as 2.1 mm), occipital 8–10 mm (CT studies).
9. Radial fractures run ahead of the bullet (PMID 2818487). Later fractures stop at earlier ones (Puppe's rule). Plates between fractures are pushed outward by pressure inside the skull.
10. 82% of 147 lethal handgun or low-velocity head shots had anterior skull-base fractures (PMID 9180024), which is what drives raccoon eyes. Clinically these appear within about 1 hour to 1–3 days (WikEM); retrobulbar bleeds measured 0.1–2.4 mL on post-mortem CT.
11. Low-energy (<550 J) brain wounds have a ~3.6 cm destruction zone around the track, with axonal damage out to 18 mm (Oehmichen 2000/2004). Handgun temporary cavities in gelatin are under 10 cm; one 5.56 study measured 17.1 cm.
12. Back-spatter (9 mm, calf heads): 31–324 macro-droplets per shot, maximum reach 72–119 cm, most within 50 cm, 13–61 m/s, emitted 0.7–4 ms after impact; micro-spatter reaches at most 69 cm and hits the gun and hand only within 40 cm (Karger, PMID 8912050 and 9081237).
13. Forward spatter runs at 47±5 m/s in a 27±9° cone; back-spatter at 24±8 m/s in a 57±7° cone; forward spatter has more droplets (Comiskey/Yarin).
14. A bullet's momentum moves an 80 kg body only 0.01–0.18 m/s, so bodies should never be thrown backwards (Karger, PMID 8956990).
15. Shotgun: a single 2.5–4 cm hole up to about 1 m, scalloped edges at 1–2 m, satellite pellets at 2–4 m, then separate pellet holes. The wad ends up inside the wound within about 1.5 m, leaves 4-petal marks (12 ga) and can mark skin out to about 6 m. 00 buck is 9 × 8.4 mm pellets; #7.5 birdshot is about 350 × 2.4 mm.
16. Facial gunshot fractures: maxilla 62%, orbit 55%, mandible 51% (578 patients); teeth and bone act as secondary missiles. Intra-oral contact shots split the lip as the lower incisors are driven forward.
17. Krönlein shot (rifle or slug at close range ejecting the brain) and the lead snowstorm (soft-point rifle only) mark the high-energy end.
18. Outcomes: 70–90% of head-shot victims die before hospital, overall mortality about 91%, bihemispheric wounds about 82%. Karger reviewed 53 cases where victims could still act after a penetrating head shot; over 70% involved low-energy .22 or 6.35 mm rounds.

Performance note for the 60 fps target: realistic spatter counts are modest (a few hundred droplets per shot), so they fit a GPU particle system with mist drawn as a few sprites.

It has 12 sections: tissue reference, sharp force, blunt soft tissue including punches, facial skeleton and teeth, skull and scalp for the hammer, thermal for the torch, a colour palette, implementation notes, a QA list, suspicious content, and references. Each of the five injury sections and the tissue reference ends with a Simulation parameters table and a Visual/behavioural checklist. Every value is tagged: [S:Rn] means sourced, [K] means my own knowledge with no source found this session, [E] means an engineering estimate or fit.

Two limits on how this was researched:
- WebFetch was blocked by the egress proxy on every domain I tried (Medscape, PMC, PubMed, forensicmed, PathologyOutlines, Wikipedia, Radiopaedia). So every sourced number comes from search-result extracts, not from reading full papers. The document lists 18 numbers for QA to check against the cited URLs first.
- The session-wide limit of 200 web searches ran out partway through the burns section. Blister timing detail, first-degree peeling, swelling heights in mm and wound-gape widths in mm are therefore [K] or [E].

Key findings:
1. Incised wounds are longer than deep; stab wounds are deeper than long. Cuts have clean edges, no tissue bridges, and a shallow tail at the end that shows stroke direction. They bleed more than lacerations because cleanly cut vessels do not constrict (Medscape R1, R3, R14).
2. Wounds across Langer's lines gape widely. Scalp wounds gape only when the galea is cut transversely (R5, R6, R7). No mm data exists in what I found, so I built a gape model [E]: G_perp 0.15–0.25 and G_par 0.03–0.05 mm of gape per mm of length. A 40 mm cut across the lines gapes about 6–10 mm.
3. A knife needs about 10–55 N to get through skin (cadaver mean 49.5 N); screwdrivers and scissors need about 3× that; skin is the main resistance (R8). A stab wound is up to 2 mm shorter than the blade width because of skin recoil (R4). On compressible areas the track can be longer than the blade (R9).
4. In 74 cut-throat autopsies, skin, platysma and external jugular were cut in 100% and deep structures in 91.9%. Deaths were exsanguination about 50%, blood aspiration 36.5%, plus some air embolism (R13).
5. Scalp vessels are tethered and cannot constrict, so scalp lacerations can cause shock (R15). A hammer case with dozens of weak blows caused death from scalp haemorrhage with no skull fracture (R55). The superficial temporal artery is 1.7–2.3 mm with about 16–18 mL/min flow per branch (R19). Normal skin bleeding time is 1–9 min (R21).
6. Bruise colour: yellow means the bruise is at least 18 h old; red, blue and purple can appear at any age up to 21 days (Langlois & Gresham, R23). The textbook chart is red 0–2 d, blue/purple 2–5, green 5–7, yellow 7–10, brown 10–14 (R25). Bruises can take up to 48 h to surface and can migrate downward (R27). Force predicts bruise appearance poorly (R28).
7. Abrasion scab: bright red under 24 h, reddish scab 10–32 h, brown 16.5–72 h, dark brown 35.5–157 h, black after 72 h. The scab is complete by 24–48 h in 93% of cases and falls off at 7–10 days (R29).
8. Lacerations have ragged, abraded edges and tissue bridges. They form over bone at the scalp, eyebrow, cheekbone, nose and chin. Shape follows the object: stellate from round objects, crescentic from a hammer edge, Y-shaped from flat surfaces (R31, R32, R35). The minimum laceration force on porcine scalp was 4 kN (R34).
9. Olympic punches measured 3427 ± 811 N at 9.14 m/s with 2.9 kg effective mass and 58 g head acceleration (R36); untrained punches are roughly 0.5–1.5 kN (weak source, R37). Facial fractures were the most common injury in 45% of one-punch assault survivors (R61). In gloved pro boxing, lacerations are 51% of injuries at 3.4 injuries per 100 rounds, and the eyebrow is 46% of eye-region injuries (R60). The per-punch damage table is [E].
10. Facial fracture thresholds: nasal 111–334 N; zygoma 0.9–2.0 kN; mandible 0.6–0.7 kN from the side and 2.4–3.1 kN at the chin; frontal bone 1.9–7.1 kN; orbital floor 1.2–1.5 J (R38–R40, R44). Assault jaw fractures are most often at the angle (R41).
11. Clinical signs: zygoma fracture shows a rim step in 100% and cheek flattening in 94% (R45). In a blowout, enophthalmos is masked by swelling for 1–2 weeks (R43). Nasal swelling hides the deformity, and clinicians reassess at 3–5 days (R46). A knocked-out tooth socket oozes for about an hour, with clot forming in 5–15 min (R48).
12. Skull fracture energy is 14–69 J overall, 22–24 J frontal and 5–15 J temporal (R55, R56). A nylon hammer delivers 70.6 J, and blow contact forces measure 2.97–4.68 kN, so one committed hammer blow can fracture the skull.
13. A depressed fracture's outer-table edge is sharp and matches the hammer face; the inner table is bevelled and wider. Angled blows give terraced fractures, and a claw leaves paired wounds (R55, R58). Pond fractures happen only in infants (R59). Surgery is indicated when depression exceeds the skull thickness or 1 cm (R57).
14. Scalp swellings: a goose egg appears in 1–5 min and peaks at 24 h (R50). Subgaleal haematomas cross suture lines; cephalhaematomas are limited by them (R49). Raccoon eyes appear at 1–3 days and spare the tarsal plate; Battle's sign takes at least 1 day; haemotympanum appears within hours (R51, R52).
15. Burns: pain starts at 44 °C; water at 60 °C for 5 s or 70 °C for 1 s gives a deep burn (R66). Heat flux of 4.5, 6.4, 10 and 16 kW/m² gives a second-degree burn in 30, 18, 10 and 5 s (R67). I fitted t2 = 10·(q/10)^−1.33 s to those four points [E]. In pigs, a 600 °C radiant source for 5, 10 and 15 s gives superficial partial, deep partial and full thickness burns (R71). Torch flames run about 1100–2000 °C (R70). The torch timeline in seconds is [E].
16. Collagen starts shrinking at 60 °C, by 30–36%, and more along Langer's lines than across them (47% vs 29%) (R73). Heat splits follow the muscle grain, are sharply edged and do not bleed (R75). Pugilistic posture took about 10 min at 670–810 °C and forms whether the person was alive or dead (R76). Bone turns brown at about 300 °C, black at 400 °C and white above 500–600 °C (R80). Smells: charcoal-like skin, sulfurous hair, beef-like muscle, pork-like fat (R78).

No suspicious or injected content was seen. Low-quality sources (punch calculators, a salon blog, a patent) are flagged in the tables. Nothing was executed, downloaded or committed, and no other files were changed.

Key findings:
1. Blood volume: adult male 70 (66–77) mL/kg, female 60–65 mL/kg. Default victim BV0 = 5.0 L (Nadler gives 5.09 L for 178 cm / 75 kg); female 3.8 L. Distribution is ~64 % veins, 13 % arteries, 7 % capillaries, 9 % lungs, 7 % heart [K-H R1, R2, R4].
2. ATLS classes (70 kg male). I ≤ 15 % (≤ 750 mL): HR < 100, RR 14–20. II 15–30 %: HR 100–120, RR 20–30, SBP normal, pulse pressure falls. III 30–40 % (1.5–2 L): HR 120–140, RR 30–40, SBP falls, confused. IV > 40 %: HR > 140, RR > 35, lethargic, grey and mottled [K-H R1].
3. Real patients are less tachycardic than ATLS predicts (Mutschler 2013, Guly 2011). Shock index ≥ 1.4 means severe shock. A biphasic vasovagal (bradycardic) faint at 20–35 % loss affects a sizeable minority (Barcroft 1944) [K-M R11–R14].
4. Section 3.3 gives a continuous lookup table by % loss (HR, BP, MAP, CO, RR, capillary refill, shock index, skin perfusion, mental state). It is fitted to ATLS, with cardiac arrest at ≥ 60 % loss, MAP < 20 for 30 s, or coronary perfusion < 15 mmHg for 60 s [G, K-M R19].
5. Consciousness is lost 5–10 s after complete loss of cerebral flow (Rossen 1943). There are 10–15 s of possible voluntary activity after the heart is destroyed (DiMaio). The brain is irreversibly injured after 4–6 min of no flow [K-H R17, R18].
6. Wound flow model: Q = 0.6·A·√(2ΔP/ρ), capped by upstream Poiseuille resistance and by cardiac output. A large arterial wound acts as a parallel shunt that drops MAP at once; for a carotid wound this gives MAP ~48–71 mmHg and 1.2–2.4 L/min [D].
7. Bleed-out times, untreated. Aorta/heart: LOC 5–30 s, death 1–5 min. Carotid: LOC 20–90 s, death 2–5 min. Common femoral: ~1.2 L/min, LOC 2–5 min, death 3–10 min. Brachial: 200–600 mL/min, death 10–30 min. Radial: usually stops by itself after 200–500 mL. Scalp: 5–30 mL/min (up to 100), keeps bleeding, Class II–III over 30–90 min [K-M + D].
8. Partial lacerations bleed more than complete transections, because transected muscular arteries retract and spasm. Elastic arteries do not stop by themselves [K-H R1].
9. Hydrostatics add 0.78 mmHg per cm below heart level. Upright neck veins and dural sinuses are sub-atmospheric (air embolism risk: 200–300 mL of air rapidly is lethal; ~100 mL/s can enter a large opening) [D, K-M R50].
10. Arterial jets: 1 mmHg = 12.8 mm of blood, so SBP 120 gives a 1.54 m ideal head. Real jets (Cv 0.6–0.8) reach 0.55–1.0 m vertically at systole and 0.35–0.65 m at diastole, and never stop between beats while DBP > ~40. As shock progresses they pulse faster and weaker, turn into welling below MAP ~25–30, and after arrest only passive gravity drainage remains [D].
11. Haemostasis: bleeding time 2–7 min, whole-blood clotting 5–15 min, serum separation from 30–60 min. Scalp vessels are held open by fibrous septa and keep bleeding. Heat or a torch seals vessels up to ~1–2 mm. Coagulopathy is present in ~24 % of severely injured patients on arrival (Brohi 2003) [K-H, K-M R31].
12. Internal bleeding: tamponade at 100–200 mL (Beck's triad, distended neck veins). Haemothorax holds 2.5–3 L per side; massive is > 1,500 mL or > 200 mL/h. Femur fracture loses 1–1.5 L, pelvis 1.5–4 L. A fist-sized clot is ≈ 400–500 mL [K-H R1, R27, R33].
13. Optics: deoxyhaemoglobin absorbs 5–10× more red light (μa per mm at 620 nm: 0.5 oxy vs 3.5 deoxy; RGB coefficients given). Section 9.3 has a hex colour table from arterial film #C0141E to pool #5E070C and venous #8E1420 [K-H R37, D].
14. Surfaces: drops ~50 µL, Ø 4.6 mm, terminal velocity 7.6 m/s. Rivulets 2–5 mm wide move at 1–5 cm/s and use 5–15 µL per cm. Pools are ~2.5 mm thick (500 mL ≈ 50 cm circle, 1 L ≈ 71 cm) and gel at 5–15 min [K-H R29, D].

I wrote the research document (about 1,450 lines, sections 0–17), but no web page could be read for it. All WebSearch calls were refused because the session's 200-search budget was already used up. All WebFetch calls were refused by the network policy: ncbi, pmc, wikipedia, librepathology, europepmc, radiopaedia, medscape and teachmeanatomy were all blocked. So every number comes from my own knowledge of standard texts and papers, and nothing was checked against a source in this session. Each value is tagged: [Cn] for a specific paper cited from memory (§16 has full citations), [D01]/[D02] for sources the earlier gunshot (01) and sharp/blunt/burn (02) research documents found by web search, [K] for textbook knowledge, [E] for derived, [G] for a game choice. Each also carries a confidence rating (H/M/L). §15 lists the 22 load-bearing numbers QA should check first. Every section ends with a Simulation parameters table and a Visual/behavioural checklist, with real time vs suggested game time.

On your 60 fps requirement: nothing in this document is expensive to run. §0.4 explains why: the physiology is a handful of numbers updated 20 times a second, the eyes are material settings, skin changes use a low-resolution mask updated at most once a second, and paralysis and rigor only change existing ragdoll joint settings.

Key findings:
1. **Brainstem (§2):** a medulla hit stops breathing at once, with no agonal gasps. Blood pressure falls to 40–60 mmHg within about a minute, and the heart keeps beating at its intrinsic rate (118.1 − 0.57 × age [C36]) until hypoxia stops it at 4–10 min. The body collapses limp in 0.6–1.2 s (0.42 s is the physical minimum) with no arm put out to break the fall. Pupils are pinpoint after a pontine hit and mid-size and fixed after a midbrain hit. Marksmen target this "T-zone" (eyes/nose/upper lip) because it is the only instant, reflex-free incapacitation [C48][C19].
2. **Hemisphere wounds (§3):** a wound in one hemisphere does not cause coma by itself. There are 53 documented cases of people still able to act after a head shot, over 70% from low-energy .22/.25 rounds [D01:S26]. Wounds crossing both hemispheres carry about 82% mortality [D01:S43]. Head impact alone can stop breathing (impact brain apnoea) [C26].
3. **Knockout (§3):** the fencing response (one arm stiffly extended, the other flexed, for a few seconds) appears in about 66% of knockouts [C20]. Concussive convulsions occur in about 1 in 70 concussions [C21].
4. **Posturing (§4):** above the red nucleus gives decorticate posture (GCS motor 3), midbrain/upper pons gives decerebrate (M2), medulla gives flaccid (M1) [C19].
5. **Seizures (§4):** tonic phase 10–20 s, clonic phase 30–60 s, about 1 min in total, eyes open in about 90% [C22][C23][C24].
6. **Raised pressure in the skull (§5):** normal ICP is 5–15 mmHg; treatment threshold is above 22 [C28]. PVI is about 25 mL [C30]. An epidural haematoma over 30 mL is operated on [C29]. Cushing's triad (high BP, slow pulse, irregular breathing) is late and appears 5–30 min before breathing stops. A breathing pattern for each brainstem level is tabulated.
7. **Spinal cord (§6):** C1–C3 stops breathing, but the victim can stay awake for 1.5–3 min and dies at 4–10 min. C4 gives see-saw breathing; C5–T1 arm function follows the ISNCSCI key muscles [C32]. Neurogenic shock occurs in about 19% of cervical, 7% of thoracic and 3% of lumbar injuries [C34]. Slow pulse is essentially universal in severe cervical injury, with cardiac arrest in about 16% [C35]. Paralysed limbs are flaccid with no reflexes for the first 24 h [C33]. A knife in the back can cause Brown-Séquard hemisection (one leg paralysed, the other numb to pain).
8. **Bleeding out (§7):** ATLS classes (under 15 / 15–30 / 30–40 / over 40% of blood volume, heart rate under 100 to over 140) [C1]. Loss of consciousness at about 40–50% loss lying down, but from 20–30% if upright. PEA arrest at about 50–60%. Paradoxical slow pulse in about a third of patients [C4][C5]. The document gives a pressure-driven bleeding model, rates per vessel and example timelines. Arterial jets stop at cardiac arrest, and exsanguinated bodies are white, not blue.
9. **Heart (§8):** 10–15 s of voluntary action after the heart is destroyed [C7][C8]. Unconsciousness comes 5–10 s (mean 6.8 s) after brain blood flow stops [C9]. In fainting, about 90% show jerks, the eyes stay open and usually roll upward [C11]. Tamponade needs only 100–200 mL of blood in the pericardium.
10. **Lung (§9):** frothy bright-red coughed blood; a chest wound over about 10–13 mm sucks air [C1]; a massive haemothorax is 1,500 mL or more; tension pneumothorax develops over minutes to hours, with low BP and tracheal shift late [C37].
11. **Agonal phase (§10):** gasping in about 30–40% or more of witnessed arrests [C12][C13]. The heart can briefly restart within about 5 min of stopping [C14]. Spinal reflex movements occur in about 40% of brain-dead patients [C16].
12. **Eyes (§11):** at death the lids stay where they were, usually partly open, and drop 2–4 mm. Inability to close the eyelids is a sign of impending death [C40][C41]. No prevalence study was found, so the 55/35/10 open/half-open/closed distribution is my game choice. The eyes do not roll up at death; that happens in fainting and seizures. They rest slightly divergent and move rigidly with the head (doll's eyes absent). Pupils dilate from 30–45 s and are fixed at 6–8 mm by 1–2 min; brain-death guidelines give 4–9 mm fixed [C17]. The surface changes follow: tear film breaks up in 10–30 s, the shine fades within an hour, corneas cloud over hours with eyes open (about 24 h closed), the dark scleral drying mark (tache noire) appears at 3–6 h, the eye goes soft within about 2 h, and vitreous potassium gives time since death (PMI = 5.26 × K − 30.9) [C46]. Brainstem eye signs are tabulated.
13. **After death (§12):** livor first appears at about 0.75 h, merges at 2.5 h, peaks at 9.5 h, shifts completely when the body is turned until about 3.75 h, and blanches completely under pressure until 5.5 h. Rigor starts at about 3 h, is full at 8 h, lasts 57 h and resolves by 76 h [C44]. Henssge's cooling formula with worked values: 20 °C air gives 34.4 °C at 6 h and 25.4 °C at 24 h [C45]. The jaw drops 10–30 mm. There is a master timeline at 120× and 720× speed.
14. **State machine (§13):** a proposed state vector, a consciousness resolver using a brain-oxygen reserve (reproduces the 10–15 s window), a transition table, 12 canonical death scenarios with real vs game times, and a tick order.
15. **§14** lists 15 common realism mistakes with fixes. **§17 (suspicious content):** none, because no web content was retrieved.

result.summary:
Yes: Godot 4.5 can hold 60 fps with heavy blood, brain and gore on a GTX 1660, if gore is built mainly from authored layers and data-driven damage masks rather than general simulation. I estimate the heavy-gore scene at 7.5–13.5 ms of GPU time on a GTX 1660 at 1080p and 4–7 ms on an RTX 3060. These are estimates only and must be profiled on real hardware. I wrote the full design to /home/user/YAYSTO/gore-game/docs/research/06_game_gore_tech.md.

How it was researched: WebSearch was unavailable (the search budget was already used up), and the proxy blocked every site except github.com and raw.githubusercontent.com. All Godot facts below were checked against the engine source, the official manual source and the website data on GitHub, including the 4.5-stable tag where versions differ. The descriptions of other games' gore systems (Dead Island 2 FLESH, Sniper Elite, Mortal Kombat, The Last of Us Part II, RDR2/Euphoria, Dead Space) come from my own knowledge and are labelled as such. Treat their details as indicative.

Key findings:
1) Godot skins characters in a compute pass before the vertex shader (skeleton.glsl, same in 4.5-stable). So VERTEX in vertex() is already skinned, and shaders cannot see bone matrices or the rest pose. Wounds should be stored in rest-pose space, with each vertex's rest position baked into CUSTOM0 at import [S2, S3, S1].
2) Godot's Decal nodes are re-projected every frame from the camera-space position through the decal box. On a character they slide as skin bends and paint through to the far side of a limb. They cannot run custom shaders or affect transparency, so they cannot cut holes. Use them only for walls, floors and brief bone-parented impact flashes. Persistent marks on the body go into textures painted in UV space [S25, S12, S6].
3) Forward+ allows 512 lights, decals and reflection probes combined per view by default, and decal cost scales with screen coverage. Visible decals are capped at about 200 and floor stains go into a floor texture instead [S6].
4) Stencil support is new in 4.5, with modes read, write, write_depth_fail and compare_*. Reads work only in the transparent pass. That suits an X-ray kill cam (the skin writes the stencil, the inner anatomy reads it) but not opaque wound holes, which use discard instead [S1, S44].
5) Shader data limits: per-instance uniforms max 16 per shader with no arrays or textures; material uniform buffers up to 64 KB on desktop. The design uses a per-character data texture for up to 64 wound volumes plus a 3D lookup grid so each pixel tests at most 4 wounds [S8].
6) GPU particles: at most 32 collision shapes and 32 attractors per system (engine constant). Signed-distance-field collision can only be baked in the editor; heightfield collision updates at runtime (256² to 8192²). Changing `amount` restarts a system, so counts are varied with `amount_ratio`. Particles cannot report collisions back to the CPU, so blood mist leaves stains as frozen stain particles, and the larger drops that must leave correct stains are simulated on the CPU with raycasts [S19, S16, S17, S14].
7) Compute shaders can feed materials only through the main rendering device, via `call_on_render_thread` and `Texture2DRD`; a separate local device cannot share textures. The official compute/texture demo shows the pattern [S37, S38, S39].
8) Subsurface scattering is Forward+ only: a two-pass screen-space blur with 11, 17 or 25 taps and a dedicated skin profile. Recommended: 17 taps on the 1660, 25 on the 3060 [S29, S33].
9) Jolt defaults in 4.5 are 10 velocity steps and 2 position steps; bodies sleep below 0.03 m/s after 0.5 s; up to 10,240 bodies. Ray hits report no triangle index unless a project setting is enabled, which costs about 25% more memory on concave shapes. Several joint parameters (softness, bias, restitution) are ignored with a warning. 6DOF springs work as Jolt position motors [S20, S5, S26, S27].
10) Scripts cannot reach the ragdoll bones' joint motors in 4.5; `get_joint_rid()` is slated for Godot 4.8. The ragdoll's muscle tone is therefore driven by spring-damper torques applied in `_integrate_forces`. Physiology sets how stiff each limb is (voluntary, weak, flaccid, rigid postures, seizure, rigor). Partial ragdolls blend through `influence` [S48, S13, S28, S4, S11].
11) Versions: Godot 4.5 was released 15 Sep 2025 (4.5.2 on 19 Mar 2026). Jolt became the default physics engine for new projects only in 4.6 (26 Jan 2026), so it must be selected explicitly in 4.5. Built-in IK nodes such as TwoBoneIK3D arrived in 4.6; 4.5 has LookAtModifier3D and BoneConstraint3D. 4.7 was released 18 Jun 2026 [S21, S22, S45].
12) Reference patterns from other engines: Raven's released GHOUL2 code puts gore marks on the posed mesh and keeps them in mesh space, with limits of 500 records and 3,000 vertices per operation [S59, S60]. Bethesda's model format pre-splits bodies into parts with authored section and torso caps for dismemberment [S61].
13) The recommended architecture: a C++ hit pipeline works out the exact hit through an invisible rest-pose copy of the body, then traces the bullet through tissue layers, bones, organs, vessels and spinal cord. Damage renders in three tiers: painted UV textures; wound volumes in the skin shader (analytic cavity for holes up to about 12 mm, discard above that); and inner meshes shown on demand (muscle shell, skeleton, skull, brain, organs, pre-fractured bones). At 2048² the body texture resolves about 0.8 mm per texel over 1.93 m² of skin, and a separate head texture about 0.24 mm.
14) Blood behaviour follows each wound's flow rate from the vessel model (doc 03): under 1 mL/min paint only; 1–15 mL/min drips; 15–300 mL/min a stream; arterial jets pulse with the heart rate, rise 0.55–1.0 m at normal blood pressure and shrink as pressure falls. Caps: 6 jets, 20 drips, 32 surface-flow agents. Rivulets are agents that walk the body surface under gravity at 1–5 cm/s with stop-start motion and drop at 30–60 µL. Floor pools spread over a floor texture at 2.5 mm thickness (500 mL is about 50 cm across) and set after 5–15 min.
15) Realism scope: pistol, knife, hammer, fist and torch essentially never sever a limb; a close shotgun blast can take fingers, a hand or wrist, or parts of the face, jaw and skull. Dismemberment is built on 12–16 pre-split zones with authored caps, and runtime cutting is limited to knife incisions in C++. Bullet momentum is small (9 mm 2.7 N·s, 00 buck 12.6 N·s, moving a 75 kg body only 0.04–0.17 m/s), so reactions come from muscle-tone changes, not knockback.
16) Content caps for a 1660: about 20k live GPU particles (40k on a 3060), at most 4 overlapping mist layers covering 15–20% of the screen (overdraw is the main GPU risk), 48 active debris bodies, and 2,000 frozen debris pieces drawn with MultiMesh in 2 m chunks. A runtime governor trims mist, particle counts, decal distance, subsurface quality and render resolution when GPU time exceeds 14 ms, and never touches wounds, physiology or the victim's stains.
17) Correction to doc 01 (gunshot wounds): its checklist says GPU particles can collide "to decals". They cannot create decals; section 8.4 of the new document gives the fix.
18) Suspicious content: no prompt-injection attempts were found. A GitHub topic listing included a repository advertising a "leaked build" of an unreleased game, a common malware lure; I did not open it or link it. README install lines were ignored. Bash was not used and nothing was downloaded or executed.

result.summary:
I could not read a single web page, so every number in the document comes from my own knowledge of the standard literature and none was checked against its source. WebSearch was refused (session budget of 200 calls already used). WebFetch was blocked by the network egress policy for Wikipedia, NCBI/PubMed, Radiopaedia, TeachMeAnatomy, Kenhub and OpenStax, and the NASA anthropometry site did not resolve. I did not try to get around the block; sibling docs 03 and 04 hit the same one. The document tags every claim ([Bn] source cited from memory, [K] textbook, [E] my own fit, [G] game choice) and gives a confidence (H/M/L). It cites 40 references with enough detail to look them up, plus an 18-item priority list for QA to verify first (§16). I found no suspicious web content, because no page content was ever returned.

corrections.claim: Bruise yellow colour indicates age >18 h; red/blue/purple can occur any time from 1 h to resolution (up to 21 d); yellow develops faster in people under 65
corrections.correct_value: >18 h for yellow confirmed. The any-time list should read red/blue/purple/BLACK, within 1 h to resolution. 'Up to 21 d' is not in the abstract as recalled; treat it as a game value.
corrections.evidence: NOT WEB-VERIFIED: WebSearch budget exhausted (200/200) and WebFetch egress-blocked on pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov and every other domain tried. Checked against the checker's recollection of the Langlois & Gresham 1991 abstract (Forensic Sci Int 50:227; 369 photos of 89 subjects; yellow >18 h; red/blue/purple/black at any time; yellow faster under 65) and Maguire et al. 2005 Arch Dis Child systematic review (yellow >18 h is the only supported colour finding). Intended source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1748358/

corrections.claim: Textbook bruise colour chart: red 0-2 d, blue/purple 2-5 d, green 5-7 d, yellow 7-10 d, brown 10-14 d (Hb, then biliverdin, then bilirubin, then haemosiderin)
corrections.correct_value: Correct as the commonly reproduced textbook/nursing chart, but it is not evidence-based. Caveat: haemosiderin-laden macrophages appear histologically from about day 2-4, so brown is not strictly last.
corrections.evidence: NOT WEB-VERIFIED (all fetches blocked). Checker's knowledge of standard forensic and nursing texts. Attribution to PMC5734826 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5734826/) not re-checked.

corrections.claim: Abrasion ageing: bright red <24 h; reddish scab 10-32 h; brown 16.5-72 h; dark brown 35.5-157 h; black >72 h; scab complete 24-48 h in 93%; scab falls off 7-10 d
corrections.correct_value: Sequence and 7-10 d scab loss are consistent with the textbook scheme (Reddy/Modi: bright red scab 12-24 h, reddish-brown 2-3 d, dark brown/black 4-7 d, falls off after about 7 d, normal colour by 2-4 wk). The study-specific hours and the 93% figure are unverified. Added Robertson & Hodge 1972 histology: epithelial regeneration from about 30 h, always by 72 h.
corrections.evidence: NOT WEB-VERIFIED; PMC5457815 and ijfcm.org blocked. Checker's textbook knowledge only.

corrections.claim: Knife skin penetration force about 10-20 N (sharp tip) up to a cadaver mean of 49.5 N (peak 55 N); skin is the most resistant layer; screwdriver or scissors need about 3x
corrections.correct_value: Qualitative points confirmed (skin is the most resistant layer; tip sharpness dominates; blunt tips need several times more force; Knight 1975). The specific 10-20 / 49.5 / 55 N and the x3 are unverified but plausible (tens of newtons). Keep the 30 N default with ±50% variation.
corrections.evidence: NOT WEB-VERIFIED; sciencedirect.com and arxiv.org blocked. Checker's recollection of Knight 1975 (Med Sci Law) and O'Callaghan et al. 1999 FSI.

corrections.claim: Stab wound skin length is up to about 2 mm shorter than blade width (elastic recoil); single-edged blade gives one acute and one squared or fish-tail end
corrections.correct_value: Confirmed. Separate correction in the file: rotating or twisting the knife gives an L/V/Y-notched wound, not a fish-tail (was 'A fish-tail also appears when the knife is rotated'). Also added: a single-edged knife can leave two acute ends when only the tip goes in.
corrections.evidence: NOT WEB-VERIFIED (forensicmed.co.uk and webpath.med.utah.edu blocked). Standard textbook content (Saukko & Knight; DiMaio): the wound is slightly shorter than the blade and must be re-apposed before measuring.

corrections.claim: Wounds across Langer's lines gape widely; scalp wounds gape when the galea is cut transversely (frontalis/occipitalis pull). mm gape model is an engineering estimate: G_perp 0.15-0.25, G_par 0.03-0.05 per mm of length
corrections.correct_value: Qualitative rules confirmed. The G coefficients remain [E] and cannot be verified (no mm data exists). Added: use Borges RSTL rather than Langer's lines for the face tension map. Flagged that Langer's classic method was round-awl punctures, not '30 mm circles'.
corrections.evidence: NOT WEB-VERIFIED; maimonidesem.org not tried because every other domain was blocked. Standard anatomy and plastic-surgery knowledge.

corrections.claim: Cut throat (74 autopsies): skin, platysma and EJV involved in 100%; larynx/trachea/carotid/IJV in 91.9%; death by exsanguination about 50%, blood aspiration 36.5%, some air embolism
corrections.correct_value: Percentages are arithmetically consistent with n = 74 (68/74 = 91.9%; 27/74 = 36.5%). CORRECTED an internal inconsistency: the text said air embolism was '19 cases', which cannot fit 74 cases with 50% + 36.5% for the other causes; the remainder is about 13.5% (about 10 cases). Added suicidal vs homicidal patterns (carotid often spared with head extension).
corrections.evidence: NOT WEB-VERIFIED; https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2090536X14000781 blocked. Arithmetic check plus textbook knowledge.

corrections.claim: Scalp lacerations can cause haemorrhagic shock because vessels are tethered in dense connective tissue and cannot constrict; bleeding resumes as blood pressure recovers
corrections.correct_value: Confirmed as stated.
corrections.evidence: NOT WEB-VERIFIED (NCBI blocked). Standard ATLS/EM teaching; the checker recalls the 'occult cause of shock' literature (PMID 10728511).

corrections.claim: Minimum force for blunt scalp laceration (porcine drop tower) was 4,000 N; the scalp tolerates dispersed force better than localized force
corrections.correct_value: Confirmed with moderate confidence as a porcine value. Added: porcine scalp is thicker and tougher than human, so the human game value is 2.5-4 kN (flat) and 1.5-3 kN (edged). Otherwise it conflicts with 2.97-4.68 kN hammer forces and with human scalp splits in falls.
corrections.evidence: NOT WEB-VERIFIED; link.springer.com blocked. Checker's recollection of the Sharkey et al. 2012 Int J Legal Med abstract.

corrections.claim: Olympic boxer punch force 3427 ± 811 N, hand velocity 9.14 m/s, effective mass 2.9 kg, head acceleration 58 g / 6343 rad/s²
corrections.correct_value: 3427 ± 811 N; 9.14 ± 2.06 m/s; 2.9 ± 2.0 kg; 58 ± 13 g; 6343 ± 1789 rad/s² (HIC about 71 ± 49). Separate CORRECTION: untrained punch force widened from 500-1500 N to 500-2500 N (default 1200), because Smith et al. 2000 J Sports Sci gives novice boxers about 2381 N.
corrections.evidence: NOT WEB-VERIFIED (PubMed blocked). High-confidence recollection of Walilko, Viano & Bir 2005 Br J Sports Med 39:710.

corrections.claim: Facial fracture thresholds: nasal 111-334 N; zygoma 900-2000 N (cadaver 930-2850 N); mandible lateral 600-700 N and frontal chin 2.4-3.1 kN; frontal bone 1.9-7.1 kN
corrections.correct_value: Nasal 111-334 N (25-75 lbf), zygoma 900-2000 N (200-450 lbf) and frontal 3.6-7.1 kN (800-1600 lbf) are consistent with the Nahum table. Mandible widened to lateral 600-1500 N (default 900) and chin/symphysis 1.9-3.1 kN (default 2.5 kN), to cover the classic Nahum/Schneider values (about 185-340 lbf lateral, 425-705 lbf symphysis, as recalled). The zygoma cadaver 930-2850 N and the frontal 50%-risk 1.9-2.4 kN are unverified.
corrections.evidence: NOT WEB-VERIFIED (PubMed and ScienceDirect blocked). Checker's recollection of the Nahum 1975 and Schneider & Nahum 1972 facial tolerance tables; lbf-to-N conversions checked arithmetically.

corrections.claim: Orbital floor (0.5 mm) blowout fracture energy about 1.22 J (hydraulic) to 1.54 J (buckling)
corrections.correct_value: Unverified. An order of magnitude of about 1 J is plausible; the 0.5 mm floor thickness is consistent with anatomy texts.
corrections.evidence: NOT WEB-VERIFIED; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16770178/ blocked. The checker could not recall the exact joule values.

corrections.claim: Skull fracture energy threshold 14.1-68.5 J overall; frontal about 22-24 J, temporal about 5-15 J; temporal squama as thin as 2.1 mm
corrections.correct_value: Overall 14-69 J is plausible (Gurdjian-era cadaver data are in the tens of joules). The temporal 5 J low end is suspiciously low (1 kg dropped 0.5 m), so the game table low end was clamped to 10 J (default 15 J) pending a source check. That the temporal squama is thinnest is confirmed; 2.1 mm is plausible, but the 4.7 mm mean may be high (about 2-4 mm typical, as recalled).
corrections.evidence: NOT WEB-VERIFIED (PMC and ResearchGate unreachable). Physics sanity check and the checker's knowledge.

corrections.claim: Hammer/implement blow energies: nylon hammer 70.6 ± 9.2 J; men 67-312 J and women 30-203 J with a 1 m striking object; hammer contact forces 2.97-4.68 kN
corrections.correct_value: Unverified, but they pass a physics check: a 0.5-1 kg head at 12-16 m/s gives 36-128 J; a 1.3 kg, 1 m tool at 20-25 m/s tip speed gives about 150-300 J.
corrections.evidence: NOT WEB-VERIFIED; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41478000/ (2025, beyond the checker's reliable recall) and /31212143/ blocked.

corrections.claim: Hammer depressed fracture: outer-table defect geometric with sharp regular edges matching the tool face; inner table bevelled and irregular; claw gives two parallel wounds; oblique blow gives concentrically terraced fracture; pond fractures are infant-only
corrections.correct_value: Confirmed. Nuances added: high energy adds radiating fractures and repeat blows give comminution; rare ping-pong fractures are reported in older children, but never in adults.
corrections.evidence: NOT WEB-VERIFIED (radiopaedia.org and pubmed blocked). Standard forensic textbook content (Saukko & Knight 'terraced fracture'; DiMaio).

corrections.claim: Raccoon eyes are delayed 1-3 days (typically 48-72 h) and spare the tarsal plate; Battle's sign takes at least 1 day; haemotympanum appears within hours; a direct black eye appears within 24 h and can cross the tarsal plate
corrections.correct_value: Confirmed. Added a small (about 10%) early-onset tail of 6-24 h for raccoon eyes after severe anterior-base injury ([K]).
corrections.evidence: NOT WEB-VERIFIED (NCBI Bookshelf and statpearls.com blocked). Standard StatPearls/EM teaching as recalled; tarsal-plate sparing is due to the orbital septum inserting on the tarsal plates.

corrections.claim: Heat flux to second-degree burn: 4.5 kW/m² about 30 s, 6.4 kW/m² blisters at 18 s, 10 kW/m² about 10 s, 16 kW/m² 5 s; fitted t2 = 10*(q/10)^-1.33 s [E]
corrections.correct_value: All four points lie on the Stoll & Chianta blister criterion (q ≈ 1.199·t^-0.706 cal/cm²s; 1.2 cal/cm² at 1 s ≈ 50 kW/m²), which gives 30.4 / 18.5 / 9.8 / 5.1 s. The [E] fit agrees within about 30% up to 150 kW/m². The Stoll form t2 = (q/50.2)^-1.416 s was added as an alternative.
corrections.evidence: NOT WEB-VERIFIED (efiling.energy.ca.gov and NIST not reachable). Independent computation from the Stoll criterion (ASTM F1930 / ISO 13506 basis) as recalled by the checker.

corrections.claim: Porcine 600 °C radiant source: 5 s superficial partial (0.4 mm), 10 s deep partial (1.3 mm), 15 s full thickness (2.4 mm); water at 60 °C for 5 s or 70 °C for 1 s gives a deep burn; pain above 44 °C
corrections.correct_value: Porcine values unverified (self-consistent with a 1.5-2.5 mm porcine dermis). 60 °C/5 s and 70 °C/1 s are confirmed. CORRECTED '44 °C pain': 44 °C is Moritz & Henriques' minimum INJURY temperature (after about 6 h); heat-pain threshold is about 43-46 °C, and the injury rate roughly doubles per °C from 44 to 51 °C. Added the M&H-derived table (49 °C 5-10 min, 52 °C 2 min, 54 °C 30 s, 60 °C 5 s, 66 °C 2 s, 70 °C 1 s).
corrections.evidence: NOT WEB-VERIFIED (PMC and PubMed blocked). Checker's recollection of Moritz & Henriques 1947 and the widely reproduced hot-water scald table.

corrections.claim: Collagen shrinks from 60 °C by 30-36%, anisotropic (47% parallel vs 29% perpendicular to Langer's lines); pugilistic posture appears after about 10 min at 670-810 °C and forms whether the person was alive or dead
corrections.correct_value: Onset at 60-65 °C confirmed. The 30-36% and 47/29% values are unverified, and PMC3924587 appears to be an organ-ablation shrinkage study, not skin. Pugilistic posture at about 10 min in a 670-810 °C furnace (Bohnert 1998) confirmed with moderate confidence; forming alive or dead is confirmed. Separate CORRECTION: bone calcination temperatures (Shipman 1984) are blue-grey 525-645 °C and white calcined above about 650 °C (was 'grey-white > 500-600 °C').
corrections.evidence: NOT WEB-VERIFIED (PMC and ScienceDirect blocked). Checker's knowledge of collagen denaturation biophysics, Bohnert, Rost & Pollak 1998, and Shipman, Foster & Schoeninger 1984 J Archaeol Sci.

gaps: NO WEB VERIFICATION WAS POSSIBLE: WebSearch reported the session budget exhausted (200/200) on the first query, and WebFetch was egress-blocked on every domain tried (PubMed, PMC, NCBI, Europe PMC, EBI, Semantic Scholar, ScienceDirect, Springer, arXiv, Wikipedia, forensicmed.co.uk, Utah WebPath, IJFCM, Radiopaedia, StatPearls). All verdicts are knowledge-based, marked '✓ verified [K-check]' or '? unverified' in the file, and must be re-checked by QA when web access exists.
Face tension map should use Borges relaxed skin tension lines (RSTL), not Langer's cadaveric lines, which diverge in the face (added to §2.3).
Stab morphology: twisting the knife gives L/V/Y-notched wounds; a single-edged knife can leave two acute ends (added to §2.5).
Suicidal vs homicidal cut-throat patterns: carotid often spared with head extension; the wound starts high on the left for a right-handed person, with tentative cuts at the start (added to §2.4).
Postmortem bruising is possible from heavy force in the first hours after death: small, non-ageing (added to §2.8 and §8 death gate).
Punch force data for novice, intermediate and elite boxers (Smith et al. 2000 J Sports Sci: about 2381 / 3722 / 4800 N) was missing; the untrained range was too low.
Stoll & Chianta second-degree burn criterion (basis of ASTM F1930) as a published alternative to the [E] power-law dose model.
Moritz & Henriques hot-water scald table (49-70 °C), and the distinction between the 44 °C injury threshold and the 43-46 °C pain threshold.
Shipman et al. 1984 bone heat-colour stages (blue-grey 525-645 °C; white calcined above about 650 °C) plus a blue-grey palette colour.
Robertson & Hodge 1972 abrasion histology staging (epithelial regeneration from about 30 h, always by 72 h; granulation 5-8 d; regression 9-12 d).
Maguire et al. 2005 systematic review: bruises cannot be aged accurately by eye; 'yellow > 18 h' is the only supported colour finding.
Human vs porcine scalp laceration threshold: the porcine 4 kN should be an upper anchor; human game values of 1.5-4 kN added so hammer blows (2.97-4.68 kN) can split the scalp.
Not re-checked beyond plausibility: hesitation-mark >70%, defence-wound percentages, ZMC sign frequencies, boxing injury rates, torch flame temperatures, 50%-risk skull fracture forces.

corrections.claim: Blood volume 70 mL/kg (M) / 65 mL/kg (F); 75 kg = 5,250 mL; ATLS classes <15/15-30/30-40/>40% with HR <100/100-120/120-140/>140; mental state anxious -> confused -> lethargic

Every cell matches the fact-checker's recall of the ATLS 9th-ed table, including RR 14-20/20-30/30-40/>35, urine >30/20-30/5-15/negligible, and 10th-ed base deficit 0 to -2 / -2 to -6 / -6 to -10 / < -10.
corrections.evidence: No URL could be opened: the WebSearch budget was exhausted, and WebFetch was EGRESS_BLOCKED on 14 domains (pubmed, ncbi, ebi, wikipedia, litfl, wikem, crossref, semanticscholar, radiopaedia, sciencedirect, merckmanuals, n.neurology.org, librepathology, bmj). Verdict rests on the fact-checker's independent recall of ATLS, not a retrieved source. File marked 'recall-consistent (not web-verified)'.

corrections.claim: LOC supine at ~40-50% loss (default 45%) or MAP <40-45 for >5-8 s; upright faint from 20-30%; PEA at ~50-60% (default 55%); PEA to asystole 2-10 min
corrections.correct_value: Defaults kept, with a note added: pulselessness can come at or below 50% loss. Recommended PEA threshold is rate-dependent: 0.45-0.50 for bleeds >500 mL/min, 0.55 for slow bleeds. The MAP trigger agrees with the ESC syncope guideline (SBP 50-60 mmHg at heart level, i.e. 30-45 at brain level upright). Separately, the §7.5 example-timeline table was corrected (see the extra entry).
corrections.evidence: No source retrievable (egress blocked). Recall: ATLS 9th-ed Class IV text says loss of >50% of blood volume causes LOC with decreased pulse and BP. Guyton & Hall (shock chapter) says cardiac output and arterial pressure both fall to zero at about 40-45% of blood volume removed over ~30 min (animal data). ESC 2018 syncope guideline (recall) gives the MAP/SBP thresholds.

corrections.claim: Paradoxical/relative bradycardia in about one third of hypotensive trauma patients; sudden decompensation at ~1-2 L equivalent central hypovolaemia in LBNP
corrections.correct_value: Prevalence possibly ~30-45%, depending on the HR cut-off (HR <=90 vs <100); flagged in the file. The LBNP part is consistent: -10 to -20 mmHg ~400-550 mL; -20 to -40 mmHg ~550-1,000 mL; beyond -40 mmHg >1,000 mL; decompensation usually at -60 to -100 mmHg.
corrections.evidence: No source retrievable. Recall only. The exact Demetriades 1998 percentage could not be pinned down, and the fact-checker's recall suggests it may exceed one third. Cooke/Ryan/Convertino 2004 LBNP-to-blood-loss mapping recalled.

corrections.claim: After the heart is destroyed there is enough cerebral oxygen for 10-15 s of full voluntary action
corrections.correct_value: Unchanged: 10-15 s (default 12). Note added that this is FBI doctrine (an upper envelope), not measured data. The original wording is '...sufficient oxygen in the brain...'.
corrections.evidence: No source retrievable. The fact-checker independently recalls the same sentence in Patrick UW, 'Handgun Wounding Factors and Effectiveness' (FBI, 1989). Consistent with Rossen 1943 (5-10 s to LOC once flow is zero) plus residual pressure decay.

corrections.claim: Complete cerebral circulatory arrest -> unconsciousness in 5-10 s (mean ~6.8 s); EEG isoelectric ~10-40 s; irreversible neuronal injury ~4-6 min
corrections.correct_value: Unchanged.
corrections.evidence: No source retrievable. Recall: Rossen, Kabat & Anderson 1943 (neck cuff; mean 6.8 s, range 5-10 s). The ESC syncope guideline (recall) cites 6-10 s of flow cessation for complete LOC. EEG silence at 10-40 s and 4-6 min neuronal injury onset are standard teaching.

corrections.claim: Syncope: myoclonic jerks ~90%, eyes open, upward eye deviation in most episodes, unconsciousness ~12 s
corrections.correct_value: Unchanged. Recall adds that upward deviation is mainly early in the episode, and hallucinations occur in ~60%.
corrections.evidence: No source retrievable. Recall of Lempert, Bauer & Schmidt 1994 Ann Neurol (56 induced syncopes) matches all four figures.

corrections.claim: Medullary destruction: immediate apnoea, no agonal gasps; MAP falls to ~40-60 mmHg; heart continues at intrinsic rate (118.1 - 0.57 x age) until hypoxic bradycardia at 3-5 min and arrest at 4-10 min
corrections.correct_value: Unchanged. The intrinsic-HR formula matches recall of Jose & Collison 1970 (=101 bpm at 30 y, arithmetic checked). Apnoea with no gasps is consistent with medullary gasp/rhythm generators. MAP 40-60 and the 3-5 / 4-10 min timings remain unverified [K].
corrections.evidence: No source retrievable. Formula recalled independently; timings have no source in either the file or the fact-checker's recall.

corrections.claim: Pontine lesion: pinpoint 1-2 mm pupils and ocular bobbing; midbrain lesion: mid-position 4-6 mm fixed pupils and CN III palsy; hemisphere lesion: conjugate deviation toward the lesion
corrections.correct_value: Unchanged. Refinement added: Plum & Posner give nuclear midbrain lesions ~4-5 mm fixed (often irregular) and pretectal lesions ~5-6 mm fixed with hippus. The 4-6 mm range covers both.
corrections.evidence: No source retrievable. Recall of Plum and Posner's classic pupil and eye-movement localisation agrees.

corrections.claim: Brain death: pupils fixed at 4-9 mm; absent corneal/oculocephalic/vestibulo-ocular/gag/cough reflexes; apnoea; eyes move rigidly with the head
corrections.correct_value: Unchanged. Added the 2023 AAN/AAP/CNS/SCCM consensus update (Greer et al., Neurology 2023) and apnoea-test thresholds: PaCO2 >=60 mmHg and >=20 mmHg above baseline (pH <=7.30 in 2023).
corrections.evidence: No source retrievable. Recall: the Wijdicks 2010 guideline states pupils are 'usually fixed in a midsize or dilated position (4-9 mm)'.

corrections.claim: At death eyelids stay where they were, usually partly open (lid drops 2-4 mm); eyes do not roll back and rest near straight ahead, slightly divergent; 'inability to close eyelids' is a specific sign of impending death; 55/35/10 split is [G]
corrections.correct_value: Citation corrected. 'Inability to close eyelids' comes from Hui et al. 2015 Cancer [C41] only (one of 8 highly specific signs of death within 3 days: nonreactive pupils, decreased response to verbal and visual stimuli, inability to close eyelids, drooping nasolabial fold, neck hyperextension, grunting of vocal cords, upper GI bleeding). It is not from Hui 2014 Oncologist [C40], which studied 10 other signs. The lid mechanics and gaze remain unverified (L-M). The distribution stays [G]; no prevalence study is known.
corrections.evidence: No source retrievable. Correction based on the fact-checker's recall of the two Hui papers' contents (medium confidence).

corrections.claim: Pupils begin dilating ~30-45 s after circulatory arrest, fixed at 6-8+ mm by 1-2 min; after death they relax to ~4-6 mm over hours and may become unequal
corrections.correct_value: Unchanged.
corrections.evidence: No source retrievable. Consistent with resuscitation teaching ('dilation begins within ~45 s, full by 1-2 min') and Knight's statement that post-mortem pupils are variable, mid-dilated and may become unequal. No primary measurement series identified.

corrections.claim: Post-mortem eye: tear film breaks 10-30 s after last blink; lustre lost minutes-1 h; corneal clouding 1-2 h / obvious 3-6 h / opaque 12-24 h open (~24 h closed); tache noire ~3-6 h (1-12) open; globe soft ~2-4 h
corrections.correct_value: Unchanged.
corrections.evidence: No source retrievable. Consistent with standard forensic teaching as recalled (clouding ~2 h open vs ~24 h closed; tache noire within a few hours, from ~3 h, eyes open). Timing is environment-dependent.

corrections.claim: Vitreous potassium rises ~0.19 mmol/L/h; PMI (h) = 5.26 x [K+] - 30.9
corrections.correct_value: Unchanged. Internally consistent: 1/0.19 = 5.26, and the intercept implies K+ ~5.9 mmol/L at death. Gap added: the 95% limits are about +/-20 h, and other formulas differ (Sturner ~0.14 mmol/L/h).
corrections.evidence: No source retrievable. Formula matches recall of Madea et al. 1989 Forensic Sci Int. Arithmetic checked by the fact-checker.

corrections.claim: Agonal gasping in ~30-40%+ of witnessed arrests, most frequent early; 2-10/min with neck extension and jaw opening, lasting 1-5 min; requires intact medulla
corrections.correct_value: Prevalence unchanged (Clark 1992 ~40%; Bobrow 2008 ~one third overall, higher with early EMS arrival). Note added that the rate (2-10/min) and duration (1-5 min) are [K], not from these papers.
corrections.evidence: No source retrievable. Prevalence figures recalled independently. The medullary origin of gasping is standard physiology.

corrections.claim: Fencing response in ~66% of knockout videos; concussive convulsions ~1 in 70 concussions (tonic up to ~20 s, jerks up to ~2-3 min)
corrections.correct_value: Unchanged. Noted that the 20 s maximum fencing duration is [G]; the source says 'several seconds'.

corrections.claim: C1-C3 complete injury: apnoea, awake until hypoxic LOC 1.5-3 min, arrest 4-10 min; phrenic C3-5; ISNCSCI key muscles C5 elbow flexion, C6 wrist extension, C7 elbow extension, C8 finger flexion, T1 finger abduction; cord ends L1-L2

corrections.correct_value: Unchanged. Gap added: Guly 2008 defined neurogenic shock as SBP <100 mmHg with HR <80 bpm; use this as the game trigger.
corrections.evidence: No source retrievable. Recall of Ditunno 2004 phases (0-1 d, 1-3 d, 1-4 wk, 1-12 mo), Guly 2008 (19.3/7/3%) and Lehmann 1987 (bradycardia in all severe cervical injuries, pressors ~68%, arrest 16%) agrees.

corrections.claim: ICP normal 5-15 mmHg, treatment threshold >22; PVI ~25 mL; EDH >30 mL operated; Cushing's triad (SBP 160-220+, HR 40-60, irregular breathing) late and pre-terminal
corrections.correct_value: Unchanged. Noted that the numeric Cushing SBP/HR bands are illustrative, not from a guideline. Added Bullock 2006 non-operative EDH criteria (<30 mL, <15 mm, <5 mm shift, GCS >8, no focal deficit). ICP example arithmetic checked (50 and 126 mmHg).
corrections.evidence: No source retrievable. Recall of BTF 4th ed (>22 mmHg), Marmarou PVI (~25-30 mL), Bullock 2006 EDH/SDH thresholds and the StatPearls Cushing reflex (full triad in about 1/3) agrees.

corrections.claim: Livor (Mallach): onset ~0.75 h (0.25-3), confluent 2.5 h, maximum 9.5 h, complete blanching until ~5.5 h, complete shift until ~3.75 h; faint after exsanguination
corrections.correct_value: Unchanged.
corrections.evidence: No source retrievable. Every mean and range matches the fact-checker's independent recall of the Henssge & Madea 2004 tabulation of Mallach's data (including incomplete blanching 17 h (10-30) and partial shift 11 h (4-24)).

corrections.claim: Rigor (Mallach): onset ~3 h (0.5-7), full ~8 h (2-20), re-forms if broken before ~8 h, persists ~57 h, resolved ~76 h; order jaw/lids -> neck -> arms -> trunk -> legs
corrections.correct_value: Unchanged.
corrections.evidence: No source retrievable. Matches recall of the Mallach data (persistence 57 h (24-96), resolution 76 h (24-192)) and Nysten's law.

corrections.claim: Henssge formula constants: Q = 1.25 exp(Bt) - 0.25 exp(5Bt) for Ta <= 23.2 C (1.11/0.11/10 above), B = -1.2815 (c*m)^-0.625 + 0.0284
corrections.correct_value: Unchanged. Gaps added: nomogram 95% limits of about +/-2.8 h (widening to +/-4.5 and +/-7 h), and a T_death state input because the model assumes 37.2 C at death.
corrections.evidence: No source retrievable. Constants match the fact-checker's recall of Henssge 1988.

corrections.claim: Henssge worked values: 75 kg body at 20 C reads 34.4 C at 6 h and 25.4 C at 24 h
corrections.correct_value: B = -0.0579 /h. Recomputed all columns: 37.1, 36.7, 35.7, 34.4, 33.1, 30.6, 27.6, 25.4, 22.7, 21.3 C at 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 12, 18, 24, 36, 48 h, all correct to 0.1 C. A related error was found and corrected in the §12.8 timeline (see the extra entry).

corrections.claim: At arrest arterial jets stop with the last beat; pressure falls to mean systemic filling pressure (~7-13 mmHg) within ~30-90 s; then gravity drainage only
corrections.correct_value: Unchanged. Guyton's ~7 mmHg is animal-derived; human post-mortem values are ~10-15 mmHg. Recalled human induced-VF data show that pressures have not equalised by 10-15 s, which is compatible with 30-90 s.
corrections.evidence: No source retrievable. Recall only; the Repessé 2015 citation details are still unconfirmed.

corrections.claim: Hydrostatics and jets: 0.78 mmHg per cm; ideal jet height at SBP 120 = 1.54 m, exit speed 5.5 m/s; real jets 0.3-1.5 m
corrections.correct_value: Physics confirmed: 1,060 x 9.81 x 0.01 = 104 Pa = 0.780 mmHg; v = sqrt(2 x 15,996 / 1,060) = 5.49 m/s; h = 1.54 m (1.03 m at 80, 0.77 m at 60 mmHg). The real-jet 0.3-1.5 m range is unverified. Gap added: use the local arterial pressure, corrected -0.78 mmHg/cm for wound height above the heart (standing neck wound ~-23 mmHg).
corrections.evidence: Arithmetic recomputed by the fact-checker.

corrections.claim: Tension pneumothorax in a spontaneously breathing victim develops over minutes-hours, with distress/tachycardia first and low BP/tracheal deviation late; open pneumothorax when wound > 2/3 tracheal diameter (~10-13 mm); massive haemothorax >=1,500 mL; each hemithorax holds ~40% of blood volume
corrections.correct_value: Unchanged. Arithmetic checked (2/3 x 15-20 mm = 10-13 mm; 40% x 5,250 = 2,100 mL). Noted that tracheal diameter varies (~13-25 mm in men), so the threshold spans ~9-17 mm; massive haemothorax is also defined as >= one-third of blood volume.
corrections.evidence: No source retrievable. Recall of Leigh-Smith & Harris 2005, the ATLS 2/3 rule and the StatPearls haemothorax '40% of circulating volume per hemithorax' agrees.

corrections.claim: (Extra) §7.5 example bleed-out timelines, e.g. 1 L/min: LOC 2.5-4 min, PEA 3.5-7 min; 100 mL/min: LOC 25-50 min, PEA 35-80 min; and §13.4 row F

Recomputed with the table's own stated method (lower bound constant flow; upper bound flow proportional to MAP from the §7.8 map_by_loss curve; LOC 45% = 2,362 mL, PEA 55% = 2,888 mL; flow-equivalent upper-bound volumes 2,800 / 3,962 mL):

- 1 L/min: LOC 2.4-2.8 min, PEA 2.9-4.0 min.

- 100 mL/min: LOC 24-28 min, PEA 29-40 min.
- 30 mL/min: LOC 1.3-1.6 h, PEA 1.6-2.2 h.
Game times were updated to match. §13.4 row F became 24-28 / 29-40 min.
corrections.evidence: Arithmetic by the fact-checker: piecewise integration of dV/(Q0 x MAP/93). The original upper bounds were 1.5-2x longer than their own stated method gives.

corrections.claim: (Extra) §12.8 timeline: rectal temperature ~35-34 C at 3-6 h
corrections.correct_value: ~36-34 C (36.3 C at 3 h, 34.4 C at 6 h for the reference body at 20 C).

corrections.correct_value: Pupil ~0.5-1 mm smaller (more obvious in dim light); ptosis 1-2 mm unchanged.

corrections.evidence: No source retrievable. Fact-checker recall of Madea's graded electrical-excitability scale (low confidence).

corrections.claim: (Extra) §3.6 'LOC >30 min means at least moderate TBI (GCS 9-12 by definition)'
corrections.correct_value: LOC >30 min indicates at least moderate TBI. LOC duration and GCS 9-12 are parallel criteria in the usual schemes (e.g. VA/DoD); one does not define the other.
corrections.evidence: No source retrievable. Fact-checker recall of standard TBI severity definitions.

gaps: NOTHING in the file has been verified against a retrieved source. Both the original author and this fact-checker were blocked (WebSearch budget exhausted; WebFetch EGRESS_BLOCKED on 14 domains). Every 'recall-consistent' item still needs a primary-source check before it is hard-coded.

Arterial jet height and bleed rate must use the local arterial pressure, hydrostatically corrected for wound height (-0.78 mmHg/cm above the heart). A standing neck wound loses ~23 mmHg; an ankle wound gains ~90 mmHg. Added to §7.6.
2023 AAN/AAP/CNS/SCCM brain-death consensus update (Greer et al., Neurology 2023) supersedes the 2010 guideline. Apnoea-test criteria: PaCO2 >=60 mmHg and >=20 above baseline. Added to §10.1 and §16.

ESC 2018 syncope guideline thresholds: 6-10 s of cerebral flow cessation, or SBP 50-60 mmHg at heart level (30-45 at brain level upright), causes LOC. Added as a corroborating source for the MAP trigger.
Loss-of-consciousness and PEA thresholds should be rate-dependent. ATLS (>50% loss -> LOC) and Guyton (output -> 0 at 40-45%) bracket them; recommend PEA 0.45-0.50 for bleeds >500 mL/min.
The Guly 2008 definition of neurogenic shock (SBP <100 with HR <80) is needed as an explicit game trigger.

Forensic readouts need error bands: vitreous K+ PMI +/-~20 h (95%); Henssge nomogram +/-2.8 h (wider with corrective factors). Henssge also needs a T_death input (hypothermic exsanguinated or hyperthermic struggling victims).
No prevalence study exists (known to either author or checker) for eyelid position at death; the open/half/closed split remains a pure design choice.
No primary measurement series was found for the time course of pupil dilation after cardiac arrest (30-45 s onset, 1-2 min full); it rests on teaching.
The exact Demetriades 1998 relative-bradycardia percentage and HR cut-off are unconfirmed and may be ~40% rather than one third.
Citation details of [C52] Repessé 2015 and the added [C53]/[C54] are from recall and unconfirmed.

corrections.claim: Blood volume: adult male 70 mL/kg (66-77), female 60-65 mL/kg; default BV0 5.0 L male, 3.8 L female; Nadler formula for procedural bodies
corrections.correct_value: Unchanged. Marino gives 66 mL/kg (lean body weight) for men and 60 mL/kg for women. BioGears uses 65.6*W^1.02 mL (about 71 mL/kg at 75 kg). The Nadler coefficients are correct, and the worked examples recompute to 5.09 L (M 178 cm / 75 kg) and 3.77 L (F 165 cm / 60 kg).
corrections.evidence: Marino, The ICU Book, hemorrhage chapter (chapter 15 in an unofficial text copy at github.com/StarleyBy/Starley-CS-Library books/icu/marino/chapters/chapter-15/chapter-15.md): '66 mL/kg (lean body weight) for males, and 60 mL/kg for females'. BioGears PatientMethodology.md (raw.githubusercontent.com/BioGearsEngine/core/master/share/doc/methodology/PatientMethodology.md): 'Bv[mL] = 65.6W^1.02', citing Morgan 2006. Identical Nadler coefficients in several independent codebases; github.com/filip-jezek/FMIComparison FMITest.mo cites 'Nadler et al. Surgery 51:224,1962'.

corrections.claim: ATLS classes: I <=15% (HR<100, RR 14-20), II 15-30% (HR 100-120, RR 20-30, SBP normal, PP down), III 30-40% (HR 120-140, RR 30-40, SBP down, confused), IV >40% (HR>140, RR>35, lethargic)
corrections.correct_value: Unchanged. Marino writes Class III as 31-40% and gives mL/kg bands: I <10, II 10-20, III 21-30, IV >30 mL/kg. Class IV 'may be irreversible'. The ATLS manual itself could not be reached.
corrections.evidence: Marino chapter 15 (same GitHub copy): Class I '<15% (or <10 mL/kg)' through Class IV '>40% (or >30 mL/kg)'. The HR/RR/UO/mental-status rows match independent teaching tables (github.com/Open-Medica/open-medical-skills skills/trauma-management-protocols/skill.py; GOATnote-Inc/openem-corpus hemorrhagic-shock.md). These are low-weight secondary sources.

corrections.claim: Real HR response is weaker than ATLS; shock index >=1.4 = severe; 25-35% of victims show biphasic bradycardic faint at 20-35% loss
corrections.correct_value: vasovagal_chance changed to 0.35-0.45 (was 0.25-0.35). In trauma patients, pulse <100 was found in 35.2% of those with SBP <100 and in 45.8% of those with SBP <90. The Mutschler citations are correct. The four SI cut-offs (0.6/1.0/1.4) remain unverified. Normal SI is 0.5-0.7.

Abstract read in the OHSUMED corpus copy at github.com/el-san59/Course_Work data/ohsu/ohsu741.json. Mutschler Crit Care 2013;17(4):R172 and Resuscitation 2013;84:309-13 confirmed via reference lists, including gdl-lang/common-clinical-models Shock_Index.v1.gdl2.json, which also gives normal SI 0.5-0.7 and >0.8 as early shock.

corrections.claim: Acute loss of >=40-50% BV is usually fatal untreated; sim arrest at >=60% loss or MAP<20 for 30 s or coronary perfusion (DBP-CVP)<15 for 60 s
corrections.correct_value: Kept 40-50% as the usual lethal range. Added Marino's caveat that 'loss of as little as 30% of the (limited) blood volume can be fatal', so fast or upright losses may kill from about 30%. The arrest thresholds are game rules; Paradis 1990 could not be reached.
corrections.evidence: Marino chapter 15 (GitHub copy): Class IV '>40%... profound hemorrhagic shock, which may be irreversible' and 'loss of as little as 30% of the (limited) blood volume can be fatal'.

corrections.claim: LOC 5-10 s after complete stop of cerebral flow; 10-15 s of possible voluntary activity after heart destroyed; irreversible brain injury after 4-6 min no-flow
corrections.correct_value: Unchanged, now marked unverified. The values are consistent with standard teaching, but no source could be reached (Rossen 1943, DiMaio).
corrections.evidence: WebSearch budget exhausted; NCBI, PMC, PubMed, Wikipedia and publisher domains blocked. GitHub code search found no text of Rossen 1943 or DiMaio.

corrections.claim: Wound flow = min(orifice Q = 0.6*A*sqrt(2*dP/rho), upstream Poiseuille supply, cardiac output); large arterial wounds are parallel shunts that collapse MAP immediately
corrections.correct_value: Unchanged. All orifice-table and Poiseuille-table values were recomputed and agree within about 1%. Also reproduced: the radial example (P_hole about 40 mmHg, about 0.56 L/min), the shunt example (P about 48 mmHg, 2.4 L/min; with tissue factor 0.2, P about 71, 1.2 L/min) and the unit conversion 1.25e-7. The model has not been validated against measured human wound flows.
corrections.evidence: Independent hand recomputation. No external data exist for this derivation.

corrections.claim: Bleed-out times untreated: aorta/heart LOC 5-30 s, death 1-5 min; carotid LOC 20-90 s, death 2-5 min; common femoral ~0.8-2 L/min, LOC 2-5 min, death 3-10 min; brachial 200-600 mL/min, death 10-30 min; radial usually self-limits after 200-500 mL
corrections.correct_value: Unchanged, but relabelled as tuning targets rather than measured facts. The rows are internally consistent with the doc's flow model and shock table: femoral 0.8-2 L/min reaches 2-2.5 L in about 1.5-4 min.
corrections.evidence: No per-vessel primary data were reachable. The only forensic survival-time abstract found (Am J Forensic Med Pathol 1988;9(3):215-7, UI 89023037, OHSUMED copy ohsu607.json) gives no numbers. Blunt aortic context: 'Traumatic rupture of the aorta: still a lethal injury', Am J Surg 1986;152(6):660-3 (UI 87073973) reports 84% overall mortality, consistent with Parmley's ~80-85%.

corrections.claim: Partial (side) arterial lacerations bleed more than complete transections because transected muscular arteries retract and spasm; elastic arteries (aorta, carotid, subclavian, iliac) do not stop spontaneously
corrections.correct_value: Unchanged, marked unverified. This is standard trauma and forensic teaching; no reachable source.
corrections.evidence: ATLS manual and forensic texts could not be reached. No GitHub-hosted primary text found.

corrections.claim: Hydrostatic correction 0.78 mmHg per cm relative to right atrium; upright neck veins/dural sinuses sub-atmospheric -> air embolism; 200-300 mL air rapidly lethal, ~100 mL/s entrainment possible
corrections.correct_value: 0.78 mmHg/cm is arithmetically correct. The 200-300 mL (3-5 mL/kg) lethal volume is confirmed. Changed '~100 mL/s through a large opening' to '>=100 mL/s', because 100 mL/s passes even a 14 G (1.8 mm) catheter at only a 5 mmHg gradient, so a torn large vein admits more.

Dog studies (Anesth Analg 1987;66:991-4 and 1989;68:298-301, OHSUMED copies) used '5 ml/kg over 30 sec' as the lethal dose.

corrections.claim: Arterial jet height: 1 mmHg = 12.8 mm blood; ideal 1.54 m at SBP 120; real jets 0.35-0.65x ideal = 0.55-1.0 m systolic / 0.35-0.65 m diastolic; no ballistic jet below MAP ~25-30; after arrest only passive gravity drainage
corrections.correct_value: Arithmetic confirmed: 133.32 Pa / (1060 x 9.81) = 12.82 mm per mmHg; Cv^2 for Cv 0.6-0.8 is 0.36-0.64; horizontal-throw times recomputed. Cv itself is a tuning value because no measured human jet heights were found.
corrections.evidence: Independent recomputation. No external measurement source found.

corrections.claim: Bleeding time 2-7 min for small wounds; whole-blood clotting 5-15 min; serum separation from 30-60 min; scalp vessels held open by fibrous septa and keep bleeding
corrections.correct_value: Lee-White whole-blood clotting time of 5-15 min is confirmed by secondary sources. The Ivy bleeding time of 2-7 min, the serum-separation timing and the scalp-septa anatomy are unverified and unchanged.
corrections.evidence: Lee-White 5-15 min in teaching notes (github.com/tapendrashahi/magic-doc normal.txt; Sakilanwar9531/Nursingmock src/blood_data.ts), low weight. The only template bleeding-time abstract found (UI 87155842) gives no range. Gray's could not be reached.

corrections.claim: Cardiac tamponade with 100-200 mL acute pericardial blood; Beck's triad with distended neck veins
corrections.correct_value: Confirmed; default 150 mL kept. Added low-pressure tamponade: in a hypovolaemic victim, venous pressures may be normal, so neck veins may not distend. The tamponade volume should be reduced by 30-50% when blood loss exceeds 20%.
corrections.evidence: Cohn, Cardiac Surgery in the Adult, chapter 57 (GitHub copy books/cardiac-surgery/cohn/chapters/chapter-57): 'Rapid accumulation of as little as 100 mL... (eg, after a penetrating cardiac wound) may... produce critical tamponade'; chronic effusions exceed 1 L; 'Low-pressure tamponade... Venous filling pressures may be normal or mildly elevated'; Beck's triad. Oxford Handbook of Critical Care (books/icu/oxford/chapters/chapter-06): 'rapid accumulations of <150mL'.

corrections.claim: Haemothorax 2.5-3 L per side; massive >1500 mL or >200 mL/h x 2-4 h; femur fracture 1-1.5 L, pelvis 1.5-4 L, tibia/humerus 0.5-0.75 L
corrections.correct_value: The massive-haemothorax thresholds are confirmed and widened: >1500 mL or more than one-third of blood volume initially, or >200-250 mL/h for 2-4 h. The 2.5-3 L pleural capacity and all fracture blood-loss figures are unverified and unchanged.
corrections.evidence: Sugarbaker, Adult Chest Surgery 2nd ed., thoracic trauma chapter (GitHub copy books/thoracic-surgery/Sugarbaker2/chapters/chapter-06): '>1500 mL upon initial chest tube insertion or more than one-third the patient's calculated blood volume'; 'output greater than 250 mL an hour for a few hours'. University of Arizona General Surgery Handbook (github.com/bilalmirza96/..., docs/Trauma/ATLS/Primary Survey.md): '>1500 mL initial output or >200 mL/hr x 4 hr'.

corrections.claim: Deoxyhaemoglobin absorbs 5-10x more red light; mu_a per mm (R,G,B) approx (0.4,28,34) arterial vs (3.0,26,50) deoxygenated
corrections.correct_value: Confirmed. Extinction coefficients (HbO2 / Hb): 450 nm 62816/103292; 540 nm 53236/46592; 600 nm 3200/14677; 620 nm 942/6510; 650 nm 368/3750. All mu_a values in the doc recompute correctly. The deoxy/oxy ratio runs from 4.6x (600 nm) to 10.2x (650 nm). Caveat added: near the Soret peaks the blue mu_a exceeds 250 per mm, so films are opaque to blue anyway.
corrections.evidence: Prahl 1999 OMLC table (Gratzer/Kollias data), copy at raw.githubusercontent.com/TimHarries/torusdata/master/prahl1999.dat. Identical rows in Nirstorm nst_get_hb_extinctions.m. The conversion formula mua = 2.303*e*x/64500 is quoted in the file header.

corrections.claim: Free-falling blood drop ~50 uL, 4.6 mm diameter, terminal velocity ~7.6 m/s; stain 3-5x drop diameter
corrections.correct_value: 50 uL and 4.6 mm are kept (the diameter is arithmetically correct). Terminal velocity changed to 7.5-9 m/s, game value 8 (was 7.6): 7.6 is the classic BPA figure but unverified, and scaled water-drop data suggest about 9 m/s. Stain spread changed to 3-5.5x (was 3-5x): the Laan correlation gives about 4.7x at a 1 m fall and about 5.6x at terminal velocity. The impact-angle formula sin(a) = W/L is confirmed.
corrections.evidence: Own recomputation with the Laan 2014 correlation (A = 1.24, mu = 4 mPa s, gamma = 56 mN/m) and a quadratic-drag fall model. Water-drop terminal velocity from memory of Gunn and Kinzer (about 9 m/s for a 4.6 mm drop); not re-fetched. Wikipedia 'Bloodstain pattern analysis' snapshot (github.com/ajb2969/MLInformationRetrieval documents/6-1285.txt): 'the width-length ratio of the ellipse is the sine of the impact angle'. No primary BPA terminal-velocity source was reachable.

corrections.claim: Blood pool on flat non-porous floor ~2.5 mm thick (capillary length 2.3 mm): 500 mL = 50 cm circle, 1 L = 71 cm, 2 L = 1 m; pool gels in 5-15 min
corrections.correct_value: Confirmed arithmetically: l_c = 2.32 mm, h = 1.6-3.3 mm, and diameters of 50 / 71 / 101 / 124 cm for 0.5 / 1 / 2 / 3 L. The gel time matches Lee-White 5-15 min. Caveat added: edge pinning may make real pools thinner (about 1.5-2 mm) and larger.
corrections.evidence: Independent recomputation. Lee-White 5-15 min from the teaching sources above.

corrections.claim: Rivulets on skin 2-5 mm wide, 1-5 cm/s on vertical skin, 5-15 uL residue per cm (a 50 uL drop runs 3-10 cm)
corrections.correct_value: Arithmetic confirmed: the Nusselt mean film speed rho*g*h^2/(3*mu) gives 2.3, 9.2 and 0.58 cm/s for h = 0.2, 0.4 and 0.1 mm. Widths and residue per cm are unvalidated estimates; contact-line pinning on skin may slow real rivulets several-fold.
corrections.evidence: Independent recomputation. No measured data found.

corrections.claim: Drying: skin smear 5-10 min; drip stain on steel 1-2 h; pool 24-72 h; colour red -> red-brown (hours, methaemoglobin) -> brown (1 day) -> black-brown (weeks)
corrections.correct_value: The chemistry sequence (oxyHb auto-oxidises to metHb, which is not reduced back ex vivo, then denatures to hemichrome, giving red to dark brown) is confirmed. All drying and colour timings are unverified and unchanged. Added the Bremmer PLoS One 2011;6(7):e21845 reference.
corrections.evidence: Wikipedia 'Bloodstain pattern analysis' snapshot on GitHub (ajb2969/MLInformationRetrieval documents/6-1285.txt), citing Bremmer et al., PLoS One 2011, doi 10.1371/journal.pone.0021845. Brutin 2011 and the Bremmer FSI papers could not be reached.

corrections.claim: Key vessel diameters: aorta 25-32 mm (infrarenal 15-20), CCA 6-8, ICA ~5, ECA ~4, vertebral ~3.5, subclavian ~8.5, brachial ~4, radial ~2.5, CFA ~8.5, SFA ~6, popliteal ~5.5, scalp/face ~2; IJV 10-20, SVC ~20, IVC ~21, CFV ~12

IVC 13-21 mm, default 17 (was 17-25, default 21; measured means 16.4-17.4 mm). Subclavian vein 7-12 mm (was 10-13). Brachiocephalic trunk length 3.5-4.5 cm (was 4-5). Confirmed: CCA 6.52 +/- 0.98 M / 6.10 +/- 0.80 F; brachial 4.36 +/- 0.87; common iliac 9.9 M / 8.8 F; descending aorta 25.8 M / 23.1 F and 24.4 +/- 3.9; infrarenal 19.3 M / 16.7 F and 18.4 / 16.6; arch 26.1 +/- 3.6; ascending about 30 (CT 36.1 M / 31.7 F); IJV 15.5 +/- 5.2; SVC 19-20.4; portal 12.1 M / 8.6 F; CFV about 14 (cadaveric). Unverified: ECA, vertebral, subclavian and axillary arteries, radial, ulnar, SFA, popliteal, tibial, scalp and face arteries.

gaps: Mean systemic filling pressure: humans measure 14-20 mmHg (ICU patients, Marino), not 7 (Guyton's animal value). msfp was changed to 10 (7-20).

Transcapillary refill can add up to about 1 L to plasma volume, and Hb/Hct do not fall visibly for 8-12 h (days to full effect). Added a refill_cap parameter and a rule to keep Hb/Hct at baseline during a session.
Hemorrhage classes expressed in mL/kg (<10, 10-20, 21-30, >30 mL/kg; Marino). Useful for procedural bodies without a blood-volume estimate.

Low-pressure tamponade: in a hypovolaemic victim a pericardial collection can have normal venous pressures and flat neck veins. The previous 'tamponade = distended neck veins' rule needs a volume-dependent exception, and the tamponade volume should drop when blood loss is high.
Massive haemothorax is also defined as more than one-third of blood volume on chest-drain insertion; the ongoing-loss threshold ranges from 200 to 250 mL/h.

Relative bradycardia is common in hypotensive trauma patients (35-46% have HR <100) and does not raise mortality. The sight of blood or a wound alone can cause a vasovagal faint (blood-injury response).

Posture changes vein size: the IJV widens 20-25% with a 15-degree head-down tilt, and the femoral vein cross-section grows about 50% with a 15-degree head-up tilt. This bears on neck-vein collapse and air entry. The subclavian vein lies about 5 mm above the apical pleura, so its wounds often involve the pleura.
Sex differences in vessel size from measured data (men's aortas 2-3 mm larger; CCA 6.5 vs 6.1 mm; CFA 9.8 vs 8.2 mm). These support the doc's 0.9x female scaling.
Blue-band caveat for the shader absorption values: near the 415-430 nm Soret peaks mu_a exceeds 250 per mm, so any blood film is opaque to blue.

Could not be verified at all (search budget exhausted, medical domains blocked): per-vessel bleed-out and incapacitation times, Rossen/DiMaio LOC timings, Mutschler SI cut-offs, Barcroft's biphasic data, Paradis coronary perfusion pressure, fracture blood losses, pleural capacity, scalp anatomy, bloodstain drying timings, drop terminal velocity, and diameters of the ECA, vertebral, radial, ulnar, SFA, popliteal, tibial and scalp/face arteries. A human with library access should check these first; they are listed in Section 16.4 of the doc.

Engine.time_scale keeps 60 physics ticks per real second (smooth slow motion without interpolation), and audio needs AudioServer.playback_speed_scale for the X-ray kill cam.

In Godot 4.5, Jolt 6DOF springs have an internal FLT_MAX torque limit that is not exposed. The 4.8 API replaces spring/motor limits with unified 'drive' limits (PR 119332), so 4.8 migration code will use new names.
Jolt contact impulses are estimated, not exact. Do not base fracture thresholds on get_contact_impulse alone.

Mist overdraw cost is mostly per-fragment lighting, not ROP/bandwidth (~0.9 ms per frame for 10 half-screen RGBA16F layers). Mist sprites should be unshaded.
